findings.title: Decision effects and infer outputs silently overwrite a person's edit
findings.claim: Automatic decision results write over fields a person set, with no conflict. Three kinds of model write apply directly through the same compare-and-set as any write: low-stakes prefills, auto-enabled effects and infer outputs. Their base is the seq the decide runner read. When a person's edit lands before the runner reads, its revision is at or below that base, so the model's write applies and replaces the person's value. Nothing excludes subjects or fields that a person has authored.
findings.evidence: architecture.md 'The write path' (lines 265-270): 'actor is a person, an auto-enabled decision effect, a prefill or an infer output -> insert edit with status applied'. 'A decision kind' (line 856): 'set_prop may set a prop or the subject's parent'. Line 826: requests are subjects 'with no decision event for their current input hash', and line 885: 'A kind-version bump ... invalidates the cache for every subject'. The `when` predicates (line 827) test only fact props such as `placed_by_rule`. I found no rule protecting person-authored fields (grep for 'person-authored field' or 'over a person' finds only scan drift, line 368). This conflicts with KICKOFF R6 ('A scan never silently overrides a person's edit'), R10 ('User-authored state is never last-writer-wins') and principle 1 ('Never lose or overwrite what someone did').
findings.failure_scenario:
1. A person moves file F, which has placed_by_rule=false, into component X (`edit move`, a set parent at seq 120).
2. The file_component request for F was still pending: no consent yet, budget spent, or the duty hadn't run. Or a later `file_component` version bump re-derives every subject.
3. The decide duty reads at seq 125. Jev picks component Y, and the low-stakes prefill commits `set parent=Y` with base 125. The person's revision is 120, which is not above 125, so the write applies.
4. F silently moves back out of X.
The same thing happens to a person's edit of a breakdown relation type (part_relation put_edge), a thread's addressed flag (commit_addresses_thread), or an infer re-segmentation over hand-edited parts (S5 'Edit a breakdown').
findings.proposed_fix: Add a person-wins rule in store::commit for every write by a model or a system decision actor, whatever the base. If any field the effect sets has a person-authored revision (an applied edit by a Person actor that no undo has reversed), the effect does not apply. Record the decision with outcome Superseded and list it in Diffs, with no card. Also make the runner's subject derivation skip subjects whose effect fields a person authored. Add tests: kernel/tests/policy.rs::a_prefill_never_overwrites_a_person_field, a_kind_version_bump_keeps_person_overrides, and an infer re-run over a hand-edited breakdown part.

findings.title: The worker's new orders client can't be linked with its truth evidence and via
findings.claim: The hint and linker rules can't derive the post-handoff `worker -> orders` http edge with the via and full evidence that TRUTH requires. The implementer's client calls HTTP through a wrapper. Method and path are arguments at the call site (line 44), and the HTTP library call (line 52) takes them as parameters. The design has no parameter binding from a call site into a hint, and no rule for normalizing an f-string path such as `/orders/{urllib.parse.quote(order_id)}/events` into a route template. So the linker either gets no path, which means no via_ref endpoint and therefore no openapi.yaml:45 or handlers.go:39 evidence, or it faces several candidate endpoints and, by its own rule, emits no edge.
findings.evidence: Fixture examples/fixture/implementer/worker-status-via-api/worker.patch, orders_client.py: line 44 `return self._request("POST", f"/orders/{urllib.parse.quote(order_id)}/events", body)`, line 52 `req = urllib.request.Request(self._base + path, data=data, method=method, ...)`, and line 39 calls GET through the same wrapper. TRUTH scenarios.S4.post_handoff.relations_added[worker->orders].evidence lists lines 44 and 52, compose:31, openapi.yaml:45 and handlers.go:39. DR-12 says 'The truth comparator requires full evidence recall'. architecture.md 'Hints and linkers': route_call attrs are `method, path, base` taken from syntax nodes. The only cross-function rule is caller call sites added as evidence (line 638), which adds lines but doesn't bind arguments. Line 640: 'A linker that finds two candidate targets emits no edge'. feature_list S4 compares post_handoff relations and relations_added, and 'done' needs the `require worker -[http]-> orders` rule to hold (architecture.md line 1080).
findings.failure_scenario:
After `handoff collect`, the hint at line 52 has base `self._base`, which resolves through ORDERS_URL to orders, but path and method are just the identifiers `path` and `method`. Two outcomes are possible:
- No endpoint can be chosen, so the edge lacks via_ref. openapi.yaml:45 and handlers.go:39 are missing, and collected_diff_equals_post_handoff fails on full recall.
- The linker treats the many orders endpoints as candidates and emits nothing. Then worker->orders is absent, the require rule doesn't hold, worker-status-via-api never becomes done, and reconciliation_after_merges_matches_truth fails.
Both are tier A failures of S4.
findings.proposed_fix: Specify a one-hop argument-binding rule in the code pack's call model. When a route_call hint's method or path is a parameter of its enclosing function, the linker resolves it from each in-container call site's literal arguments (`code.call` with argument captures), producing one route_call per call site, and records both the call site and the wrapped call as evidence. Also specify path normalization: an interpolation segment becomes `{}` and matches any `{param}` segment of a served route. Add extract/tests/link.rs::a_wrapper_call_binds_method_and_path and a fixture test that line 44 yields `POST /orders/{id}/events` and line 39 yields `GET /orders/{id}`. If this can't be built, file the KICKOFF infeasibility record now (Biggest bet 5), not at M2.

findings.title: Flushing another tab's pending edits uses an unspecified writer instance
findings.claim: The design says any signed-in tab flushes the workspace's pending canvas edits 'with their original keys'. It says nothing about the client ID, so presumably the flushing tab sends its own tab ID. Compare-and-set compares writer instances and 'a writer instance never conflicts with its own later writes'. So a stale edit from tab A, flushed by tab B, is checked as if B wrote it, and it silently overwrites B's own newer value for that field. If the client is part of the request hash, a flush of an edit that already committed returns idempotency_mismatch instead of replaying.
findings.evidence: architecture.md 'The canvas' > Writes (line 1309): 'Each tab mints a tab ID and sends it with every write as its client ID ... Any signed-in tab of that workspace flushes them with their original keys'. 'Actors' (line 401): the client ID is a canvas tab's ID, and 'Conflicts compare writer instances'. 'Conflicts' (line 434): 'A writer instance never conflicts with its own later writes'. DR-8 round 2 moved pending edits to localStorage for cross-tab flushing. KICKOFF R10: 'No write is lost ... User-authored state is never last-writer-wins'.
findings.failure_scenario: Tab A renames block K to 'Bag' from base 100, then A is closed (or serve restarts) before the reply. A's edit sits in localStorage. Meanwhile tab B, already open, renamed K to 'Basket' at seq 105. B notices A's pending entry and flushes it with client tab_B and base 100. rev(K.name)=105 was written by tab_B, the same writer instance, so there is no conflict. 'Bag' applies over 'Basket', and no card shows, although the two edits were concurrent.
findings.proposed_fix: Store each pending edit with its full original WriteCommon: client (the minting tab's ID), base, idem and request body. A flush sends that client unchanged, and the engine accepts a client ID other than the flusher's only for a resend from the pending store, under the same person bearer token. Define request_hash over the command, args, base, actor and client, never over transport fields. Add tests/e2e/surface.spec.ts::a_flush_by_another_tab_keeps_the_original_writer (expect a stale_write card) and ::a_flush_of_a_committed_edit_replays.

findings.title: The restore replay set re-commits edits with bases from another seq timeline
findings.claim: `doctor --restore` sets aside the events above the restored copy's last seq L and later replays them 'through store::commit with each event's actor and idem'. Those events carry `base` values from the abandoned timeline, while the restored store reuses seqs L+1 and up for new edits. Compare-and-set therefore compares numbers from two unrelated timelines. A set-aside edit can silently overwrite an edit the person made after the restore, or raise spurious conflicts. The same problem hits the git-clean restore path. Scan events and reconcile outcomes name integer snapshot IDs, `Scan.snapshot` and `link`, which mean nothing, or something else, in a freshly scanned store. So 'resolved stays done' classes and plan version tags aren't faithfully restored.
findings.evidence: architecture.md line 504 ('The next successful migration replays the set through store::commit with each event's actor and idem ... a stale event becomes a person conflict card'). contracts.md line 334. contracts.md Edit.base is a Seq (line 478). EventBody::Scan holds `snapshot: u64, link: u64` (lines 466-467), and the snapshots table uses `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`. Line 501: 'A restore sorts by the original seq and dedupes by idem'. KICKOFF principle 1: 'Never lose or overwrite what someone did'.
findings.failure_scenario:
1. On v0.2 the person renames K at v0.2-seq 260 (base 255), then downgrades with `doctor --restore`. The restored copy ends at L=240, and 260 goes into the replay set.
2. On v0.1 the person renames K again at seq 243.
3. On upgrade, the replay commits the v0.2 rename with base 255. rev(K.name)=243 is below 255, so there is no conflict, and the older v0.2 rename overwrites the person's newer post-restore rename with no card.
Separately, a git-clean restore that replays a Scan event naming snapshot 3 points the fold at whatever snapshot now has ID 3.
findings.proposed_fix:
Define replay semantics explicitly:
- When replaying a set-aside or backed-up event through store::commit, rebase its `base` to the last seq both timelines share (L for a replay set, the restore's starting seq for a git-clean restore). Any post-restore write to the same field then conflicts and becomes a person card.
- Never replay scan or decision events. Re-derive them by rescanning.
- Carry reconcile classes and version tags in an engine-written 'restored outcome' event, keyed by item and commit, not by snapshot ID.
- Preserve the stored status of events that were conflicts.
Add backup.rs::a_replayed_edit_conflicts_with_a_post_restore_edit and ::a_restore_keeps_done_classes.

findings.title: The reconciler misclassifies when a hand-off merge and a regressing commit land in one window
findings.claim: Rule 1 classifies a regression only against a rule 'that held at the previous reconciled snapshot', and rule 2 needs all rules to hold at the head. If the hand-off merge and a commit that breaks its rule both arrive before the next scan, the rule never held at a window start. The regression goes unseen, the item never becomes done, and both units fall through to reconcile.residual cards. S4's CI path passes only because it puts a scan between the merges.
findings.evidence: architecture.md 'The reconciler' rules 1-2 (lines 1079-1080), and change units are 'git log --no-merges prev..head' (line 1076). feature_list.json S4 steps place 'planroom scan --json' between `handoff merge` and the teammates merges. TRUTH reconciliation_rules state regression-over-unplanned and resolved-stays-done as general rules. KICKOFF R7 ('on demand and on change') and principle 1 (cards only for decisions only a person can make).
findings.failure_scenario:
The person merges the hand-off from the pane, then immediately runs `git pull`, which brings in teammates' 'Write audit rows straight to orders-db'. The next scan sees both:
- The forbid rule is broken at the head and didn't hold at the window start.
- worker-status-via-api isn't done, isn't in progress (merged) and isn't expected (started), so it goes residual.
- The audit commit breaks a rule, so it isn't unplanned, and it didn't break a rule that held, so it isn't a regression either. It also goes residual.
Result: two spurious cards instead of done plus regression.
findings.proposed_fix: Evaluate the window per change unit in topological order: apply each unit's attributed fact delta in turn, and classify a unit as a regression when it breaks a rule that held just before it, including a rule an earlier unit in the same window made hold (such as the hand-off's commits). Mark an item done at the first point in the window where its rules all hold and its branches are merged. Add kernel/tests/reconcile.rs::handoff_and_regression_in_one_window.

findings.title: The roll-up rule contradicts its own internal-count rule
findings.claim: As written, an end of an edge never lifts to an ancestor of the other end and 'stops at that ancestor's child on its own path'. When both ends lift to the same ancestor C, C is an ancestor of the other end, so both ends stop at C's children. Applied recursively, that pushes them down to the original nodes. So no edge ever becomes C's `internal` count, and maps at higher levels pull in lower-level nodes, such as file-to-file imports on a Component map. That contradicts the next bullet, and S1 ('faithful roll-ups') rests on one definition of lift.
findings.evidence: architecture.md 'Levels and roll-ups' line 321 (the never-to-an-ancestor rule) versus line 323 ('Edges inside one ancestor become that ancestor's internal count, not self-loops'). The faithfulness property test (line 322) passes under either reading, so it won't catch the divergence. KICKOFF R1 and S1.
findings.failure_scenario: On the dependencies lens at Component level, two files in storefront/src/cart import each other. Literal rule: both ends stop at cart's children, so the Component map draws two Code-level file nodes and an edge, not 'cart: 1 internal'. The canvas, the mini-map and `map --detail summary` disagree depending on which bullet each implementer followed.
findings.proposed_fix:
State lift precisely:
- Let a and b be each end's nearest ancestor at or above the level.
- If a == b, count the edge as a's internal.
- Else if a is an ancestor of b's original end, replace a with a's child on that end's path. Do the same for b.
- Never descend below the level otherwise.
Add rollup.rs::same_ancestor_edges_are_internal, and keep the orders(repo) -> redis example as a test.

findings.title: No commit-time store-version check stops an older process writing after a migration
findings.claim: The design says an older watch or serve 'exits with schema_mismatch after a migration'. It doesn't say the check happens inside every store::commit transaction. A watch from another session can run a duty (a rescan or decide run) that commits after a newer binary has migrated. That writes old-shaped rows into the migrated store, or commits against changed semantics, before the poller notices.
findings.evidence: DR-1 decision ('an older watch or serve exits with schema_mismatch after a migration'). architecture.md line 1229 (Version handshake), and lines 155 and 164: watch runs duties that commit facts and events. The 'drains older serve' step covers serve only, not watch processes in other sessions or one-shot CLIs already running.
findings.failure_scenario: Session 1 (v0.1) has a watch mid-rescan of orders. Session 2 (v0.2) migrates the events table in one transaction. The rescan's BEGIN IMMEDIATE waits on the 5 s busy timeout, then commits with v0.1 column assumptions into the v0.2 store. The events backup then copies those rows, and the next v0.2 fold misreads them or fails.
findings.proposed_fix: Inside every store::commit and every duty transaction, read `PRAGMA user_version` (or meta.store_version) after BEGIN IMMEDIATE and abort with schema_mismatch when it isn't the process's own version. Add store/tests/migrate.rs::an_older_writer_refuses_after_a_concurrent_migration.

findings.title: One-shot reads don't pin the fold and meta.seq to one read transaction
findings.claim: Every one-shot command folds from scratch over several queries (scan events, snapshots, facts, events) and returns meta.seq, which writers then send back as base. The design never says these reads share one WAL read transaction. If meta.seq is read after a concurrent commit that the fold missed, the next write's base covers a change the writer never saw, which is a silent lost update. Snapshot pruning between queries, or between pages of a cursor over `(seq, last_id)`, can also delete facts that fold(at=N) needs.
findings.evidence: architecture.md line 373 ('One-shot commands fold from scratch'), line 381 (snapshots 'pruned after the last 20 per repo'), and line 1204 (cursor 'consistent with the version it started at'). A grep for 'read transaction' or 'snapshot isolation' finds nothing. KICKOFF S8: 'a stale write becomes a diff rather than a merge'.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent's `show K` reads events up to seq 300. A canvas rename of K commits at 301. `show` then computes meta.seq = max(seq) = 301 and returns the old name with seq 301. The agent proposes a rename with base 301, so no conflict and no three-way diff are reported, although the agent never saw the 301 rename. With person actors (the mod's base defaults), the same race makes a stale person write apply.
findings.proposed_fix: Have every read open one deferred read transaction, set N = max(seq) inside it, run fold(at=N) entirely inside it, and return meta.seq = N. Make pruning refuse to delete snapshots referenced by any scan event within the newest K seqs, and have a cursor read return `reset` when its snapshot is gone. Add store/tests/interleavings.rs::meta_seq_never_exceeds_the_folded_view.

findings.title: The decide lease is keyed by the request-set hash, so overlapping runs can collide
findings.claim: The decide duty's lease is named `decide:<requests hash>`. Two processes that derive slightly different pending sets, for example one before and one after a scan, take different leases and both run Jev on the subjects they share. A decision event's idem is sha256(kind, version, subject, input_hash), so the second commit hits the same idem. If Jev's answer differs (the design cites +/-0.05 drift), the request hash differs, the commit gets idempotency_mismatch, and the second runner's transaction can roll back its other decisions too. The spend is wasted either way.
findings.evidence: architecture.md 'Duties' (line 164: lease names such as `decide:<requests hash>`), 'Idempotency and retries' (line 444: the decision key; line 446: 'same idem with a different hash is idempotency_mismatch'), and line 941 (Jev drift +/-0.05). KICKOFF S7: under $0.001 per routine rescan.
findings.failure_scenario: The watch in session 1 and `planroom decide --run` from an agent start together after a rescan. Their request sets differ by one subject, so they hold two leases. Both call Jev for the 12 shared subjects and double the cost. The second commit hits idempotency_mismatch on the first decision event and aborts, which loses its 13th decision until the next run.
findings.proposed_fix: Use one `decide` lease per workspace, or per (kind, subject) partition. Define a decision event's request hash over its inputs only (kind, version, subject, input_hash), not the model's answer, so a duplicate replays. Make the runner skip a subject whose decision event already exists inside its commit transaction. Add duties.rs::concurrent_decide_runs_ask_each_subject_once.

findings.title: architecture.md still says S7's rescan skips the reconciler, contradicting DR-72
findings.claim: The 'at most one card' argument for S7 in architecture.md says the rescan checks out `routine` off the tracked branch, so the reconciler skips storefront. DR-72 and feature_list.json changed S7 to a fast-forward merge of routine into main, so the reconciler does run, and the routine commit is classified (unplanned). The written argument for S7's tier A card bound rests on the superseded path.
findings.evidence: architecture.md line 885 ('The rescan checks out `routine`, which isn't storefront's tracked branch, so the reconciler skips that repo and deals nothing [DR-71]'). decisions.md DR-72 ('S7's commit-triggered rescan is a fast-forward merge of `routine` into `main` ... so the tracked branch moves and the reconciler runs'). feature_list.json S7 step 'git -C $OUT/storefront merge --ff-only routine'.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer follows architecture.md and makes the S7 test check out `routine`. The reconciler path that S7 is now meant to exercise is never tested. Or someone reasons from the stale text that no reconcile class can appear, and misses that the unplanned unit must raise no card (rule 5 must stay card-free), so routine_rescan_at_most_one_card can regress unseen.
findings.proposed_fix: Rewrite line 885: the ff-merge moves main, the reconciler runs, the routine commit is classified `unplanned`, and unplanned units appear in Diffs and never deal a card. That keeps the bound at one possible card, a regression. Add an assertion to s07_decisions.rs that the reconcile outcome on the last scan event lists the routine commit as unplanned.

verdicts.reason: Nothing in the design keeps a decision effect, prefill or infer output from overwriting a field a person set. Compare-and-set only conflicts when a field's revision is above the writer's base and was set by another writer instance. The decide runner reads after the person's edit, so its base covers that edit and the effect applies. The only protection against overwriting a person is for scans (fold step 5) and for `retarget`. No `when` predicate looks at overrides: `placed_by_rule` is a fact prop the `files` extractor sets. Worse, if the slice includes `parent`, a person's move changes the input hash and raises a fresh request, which then overwrites the move. This breaks principle 1 and R10 ('never last-writer-wins'), so it is material.
verdicts.evidence: architecture.md:269 write path: 'else actor is a person, an auto-enabled decision effect, a prefill or an infer output -> insert edit with status applied'; :431 'A write conflicts when a field it sets has rev > base, written by a different writer instance'; :826 requests are subjects 'with no decision event for their current input hash: sha256 of the kind, its version, the questions and the serialized slice'; :827 `placed_by_rule` is 'set by `files`'; :856 '`set_prop` may set a prop or the subject's `parent`'. The only person-protection rules are :368 (scan drift) and :856 (retarget needs a person). A grep of decisions.md for override or person-edit protection finds none for decision effects. KICKOFF.md:39 'Never lose or overwrite what someone did'; :89 R10.

verdicts.reason: The fixture wrapper takes method and path as parameters at line 52. The literal method and the f-string path appear only at call sites (lines 39 and 44). The design's hint table gives `route_call` attrs `method, path, base` from 'fetch templates, HTTP clients'. Its only cross-function rule adds callers' lines as evidence. Nothing binds arguments from a call site into the wrapped call's hint, and nothing normalizes `f"/orders/{urllib.parse.quote(order_id)}/events"` to `/orders/{id}/events`. So the linker can't pick the `POST /orders/{id}/events` endpoint for `via_ref`. Without `via_ref`, openapi.yaml:45 and handlers.go:39 are missing, and DR-12 requires full evidence recall. Or the linker emits no edge because it has several candidates. Either way S4, a tier A scenario, fails. The design's own risk R-3 admits joins like this may be missing, but it doesn't specify this one.
verdicts.evidence: worker.patch, orders_client.py: line 44 `return self._request("POST", f"/orders/{urllib.parse.quote(order_id)}/events", body)`; line 52 `req = urllib.request.Request(self._base + path, data=data, method=method, headers=headers)`. TRUTH.scenarios.S4.post_handoff.relations_added[worker->orders] has via 'POST /orders/{id}/events' and evidence at lines 44 and 52, compose:31, openapi.yaml:45 and handlers.go:39. architecture.md:628 route_call attrs; :638 caller call sites are added only as evidence; :640 'A linker that finds two candidate targets emits no edge'. decisions.md:332 full evidence recall. A grep for wrapper, argument or interpolation finds no binding rule. feature_list S4 is tier A.

verdicts.reason: The design stores and resends only the original `idem` with a pending edit. Its stated rule is that each tab sends its own tab ID as the client ID with every write. Read literally, a flush by tab B carries tab_B as the client. Compare-and-set compares writer instances, and 'a writer instance never conflicts with its own later writes'. So tab A's stale edit, flushed by B, silently overwrites B's newer value for that field. That is a person's edit lost under last-writer-wins, against R10 and principle 1. The case is a closed tab, a reload or a serve restart while another tab is open, which is exactly what the localStorage flush exists for. Neither the contracts nor DR-8 say the original client is kept.
verdicts.evidence: architecture.md:1309 'Each tab mints a tab ID and sends it with every write as its client ID ... Pending edits live in localStorage ... each with the idem it was minted with. Any signed-in tab of that workspace flushes them with their original keys'; :401 'Conflicts compare writer instances'; :434 'A writer instance never conflicts with its own later writes'. contracts.md:254 WriteCommon.client is 'the client ID of the writer instance: a canvas tab'. decisions.md:274 (DR-8 round 2) mentions only 'their original keys'. KICKOFF.md:89.

verdicts.reason: The replay set's events carry `base` values from the abandoned v0.2 timeline. The restored copy's AUTOINCREMENT sequence resumes at L+1, so post-restore edits reuse those seq numbers. When the replay goes 'through store::commit with each event's actor and idem', compare-and-set compares numbers from unrelated timelines. A v0.2 edit with base 255 sees rev 243 as not newer, and it applies over the person's later post-restore edit with no card. That defeats the design's own claim that 'a stale event becomes a person conflict card'. It loses a person's edit, which is a data-loss risk. The backup also appends 'every event above the high-water seq', scan events included, and those name integer snapshot IDs that mean nothing in a rebuilt store. So the second half of the finding is plausible too.
verdicts.evidence: architecture.md:504 'The next successful migration replays the set through store::commit with each event's actor and idem ... and a stale event becomes a person conflict card'; :501 'appends every event above the high-water seq ... A restore sorts by the original seq and dedupes by idem'; :463 `events (seq INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT`; :467 `snapshots (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`. contracts.md:334; contracts.md Edit.base: Seq; EventBody::Scan { snapshot: u64, link: u64 }. No rule rebases a replayed edit's base.

verdicts.reason: Real, and already rated minor. Rule 1 needs a rule that 'held at the previous reconciled snapshot'. Rule 2 needs every rule to hold at the head. Change units are all the non-merge commits since prev, and the delta runs from prev to head. In the fixture, the forbid rule (worker -db-> orders-db) is broken on main before the hand-off. If the hand-off merge and the teammates merge land in one window, the rule is broken both at the window start and at the head. Then the regression isn't recognized, done doesn't fire, and residual cards follow. The S4 CI path puts a scan between the merges, so tier A passes. That keeps it minor.
verdicts.evidence: architecture.md:1075-1084: change units from 'git log --no-merges prev..head'; the fact delta runs 'from the previous reconciled snapshots to the current head snapshots'; rule 1 'breaks an intended rule that held at the previous reconciled snapshot'; rule 2 'An item whose rules all hold'; rule 6 residual card. feature_list S4 steps run 'planroom scan --json' after `handoff merge` and before the harness's teammates merges. No per-unit sequential evaluation is specified.

verdicts.reason: The two bullets do conflict as written. When both ends' nearest ancestor at the level is the same node C, C is an ancestor of the other end, so the 'never to an ancestor of the other end' clause stops each end at C's child. That contradicts the next bullet, which makes such edges C's `internal` count. A careful implementer could read the internal-count bullet as the exception, so this is ambiguity rather than a certain failure. The faithfulness property test passes under either reading, so it won't catch the divergence. Minor.
verdicts.evidence: architecture.md:321 '...lifted to the nearest ancestor of each end at or above `level`, but never to an ancestor of the other end: such an end stops at that ancestor's child on its own path'; :323 'Edges inside one ancestor become that ancestor's `internal` count, not self-loops'; :322 the faithfulness invariant is independent of which reading applies.

verdicts.reason: The design says an older watch or serve exits with schema_mismatch after a migration, and that a newer binary drains an older serve before migrating. It never says the store version is checked inside each commit transaction. An older watch in another session, or a one-shot command already past its open check, can commit a duty's rows after the migration. The packs check has an equivalent ('refuses writes with packs_mismatch'), but the schema version has none. Minor, as rated.
verdicts.evidence: decisions.md:123 'an older `watch` or `serve` exits with `schema_mismatch` after a migration'; architecture.md:1229 'A newer binary also drains an older `serve` before migrating the store. After a migration, a `watch` or `serve` of an older version exits with `schema_mismatch`' (serve is drained, watch isn't); :164 watch runs duties that commit; contracts.md:334 the check is described only at store open. A grep for user_version or store_version finds no per-transaction check.

verdicts.reason: The design never says a one-shot read runs its fold and computes meta.seq inside one read transaction. If they run in separate implicit transactions, meta.seq can exceed the folded view. The writer then sends a base that covers a write it never saw, and compare-and-set lets a stale write apply. That is the lost update S8 guards against. The cursor's 'consistent with the version it started at' says nothing about pruned snapshots. This is an implementation-specification gap that a careful implementer would probably close, so minor, as rated.
